narrative:
The model predicted a 61% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three pieces of information about your academic record. Your class ranking in the third year of law school was the strongest factor and pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. You placed in the bottom decile (1 out of 10), while students who were accepted averaged around the middle of their class (5.8). This low ranking signaled to the model a higher risk of struggling on the bar.

Your first-year class ranking was the third most important factor and also pulled the prediction toward failure. You again ranked in the bottom decile (2 out of 10), compared with an average of 6.0 among accepted students.

Your LSAT score of 37 was the second most important feature, but it worked in the opposite direction. This score is almost exactly the same as the average for accepted students (37.18), so it helped offset some of the risk created by your class rankings and nudged the prediction slightly toward passing.

Taken together, the model concluded that your relatively low class standings outweighed the solid LSAT performance, producing an overall prediction of likely bar exam failure.

What you should do next is focus on strengthening your academic performance and consider retaking the bar-prep courses that target the specific subjects where your grades were weakest. Improving your class rank in the remaining year could substantially change future predictions.
